newsitem.title: UK: UK's Ofgas considers ending daily balancing regime.
newsitem.headline: UK's Ofgas considers ending daily balancing regime.

text.p: The UK natural gas market's balancing regime needs improvements ahead of the coming winter, according to a consultation document published by industry regulator Ofgas on Tuesday.
In the long term, Ofgas will consider whether daily balancing, ensuring that inputs to the pipeline system and offtakes by customers are balanced every day, is necessary at all.

"Other gas transportation systems, for example in the United States, balance on a daily basis on peak days only. Ofgas will be considering whether there is a compelling need for the system to continue to be balanced on a daily basis every day," the report, "The Gas Balancing Regime" said.
Ofgas started a review of the gas balancing system in March 1997.

It was intended to look at how the system had worked during the first winter since the Network Code was signed -- the standard contract between pipeline operator BG plc unit Transco and gas shippers that use the system.
Under the code, Transco is responsible for overall balance but each individual shipper is responsible for controlling how much gas it puts in, and for monitoring how much their customers take out.
Any imbalance is bought or sold on a daily basis by Transco.

The main instrument for preserving the balance is the Flexibility Mechanism, a screen-based trading system which allows shippers to provide gas to the system or take it off the system by posting bids on screen.
If Transco needs to balance it will accept bids in price order (lowest price bids when the system is buying, highest bids when selling) up to the required volume.
Prices on the flexibility mechanism are used to determined the System Average Price (SAP) at which shipper imbalances are cashed out, or charged.
If imbalances are outside a certain tolerance level, these charges are higher, at the System Marginal Price (SMP), or the level of the marginal bid accepted by Transco.
The Ofgas document concluded that there has been active participation on the flexibility mechanism over the first winter, and that delivery of bids by shippers has been "generally good."

But the report noted that the amount of gas available to be bought or sold is normally highest at the start of the day and decreases fairly consistently towards its end. As there tends to be less gas available then, if Transco needed to balance then, "volatile prices could result."
And the report also notes that arbitrary cash-out prices have been seen, as "the prices generated from the flexibility mechanism do not necessarily reflect supply and demand conditions on the day."

Transco has put forward some proposals for changes to the balancing regime in the short term, saying the review suggests that "it would be beneficial to consider making some improvements to the regime before winter 1997/98."

These include setting up a supply side forum to address information flows between producers and Transco; allowing extra flexibility during the day so that shippers can renominate more frequently; allowing bids to be taken for flexibility on the day ahead; capping imbalance prices; and addressing incentives not to balance on a daily basis.
In the longer term, Ofgas is looking at ending the need for daily balancing by Transco and by individual shippers.
Ofgas is also pondering ending Transco's revenue neutrality, saying "it may be appropriate for Transco to be given a clearer commercial incentive to optimise system balancing costs."
The regulator will also be looking at the flow of information between offshore and onshore market participants to ensure efficient operation of the pipeline system.
Ofgas will also consider interactions between gas and electricity, given that a growing proportion of electricity generation comes from gas fired power stations.
